food.text: Aboriginal Australians ate native animal and plant foods across an estimated 60,000 years of human habitation on the continent. One estimate counts 4,999 species of native food used by Aboriginal peoples, drawn from the plants and animals of each region.

Bush tucker covers a wide range of foods. Animal foods include kangaroo, emu, witchetty grubs and crocodile, while plant foods include the fruits quandong and kutjera, the spice lemon myrtle, warrigal greens and various native yams.

Traditional Aboriginal society had a cooperative economy in which males generally hunted large game. Females gathered local staples such as small animals, shellfish, vegetables, fruits, seeds and nuts. Food was shared within groups and exchanged across groups.
Aboriginal star lore worked as a food calendar. Stars or constellations rising or setting told people when to move to a new place or look for a new food source, and stories carried this knowledge.

Much native food was unsafe or unpalatable raw, so it was processed before eating. Methods included cooking on open fires, boiling in bark containers, pounding vegetables and seeds, and hanging bags in running water. Toxic seeds, such as Cycas media and Moreton Bay chestnut, had to be processed to remove the toxins and render them safe to eat. Some animals, such as kangaroos, were cooked in their own skins, and others, such as turtles, in their own shells.

Some Aboriginal groups practised fire-stick farming and fish farming, and built semi-permanent shelters. How far some groups engaged in agriculture is controversial, and some anthropologists call traditional Aboriginal Australia a "complex hunter-gatherer" society.

Bush tucker also included nuts and fungi. The bunya nut and the macadamia nut are among the native nuts, and although knowledge of Aboriginal uses of fungi is meagre, beefsteak fungus and native "bread", itself a fungus, were certainly eaten.

The Boorong people of Victoria watch for the Malleefowl (Lyra) to disappear in October, when it goes to "sit with the Sun". That is their signal that it is time to start gathering the malleefowl's eggs on Earth.

The Yamatji people of the Wajarri language group, in the Murchison region of Western Australia, call the sisters Nyarluwarri. When the constellation is near the horizon at sunset, they know it is the right time to harvest emu eggs.

The Yolŋu people of northern Australia see Orion, which they call Julpan, as a canoe. In their story, one of three fishing brothers ate a sawfish forbidden under their law, so the Sun-woman, Walu, lifted all three and their canoe into the sky with a waterspout.
